newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: IMF to determine fate of key Cambodian loans.
newsitem.headline: IMF to determine fate of key Cambodian loans.

text.p: A four-member delegation from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is scheduled to arrive in Cambodia on Monday to determine the fate of $40 million in important loans, officials said at the weekend.
"We're discussing a possible third annual arrangement under the programme approved by our board in May of 1994," said Resident Representative Joshua Charap of the 10-day mission.
Officials said it was an anxious time for the Cambodian government, which derives about 40 percent of its budget from foreign aid.
"(The IMF decision) will be very important for the economic development of Cambodia, and also the reputation and the feasibility of Cambodia," said Foreign Minister Ung Huot.

Last November, the government was shaken by the IMF's decision to cancel a $20 million disbursement over perceived problems with accounting procedures for logging revenues and the national forestry policy.

They must now prove they have rectified the problems or face the suspension or cancellation of the last year of the IMF's, $120 million loan programme, which consists of two, $20 million payments each year.
Half the $120 million has been disbursed, but the $20 million payment last November lapsed and the fate of the remaining $40 million remains uncertain.

Michael Kuhn, assistant director of the IMF's Central Asia Department, said in November that the $40 million would be partly contingent upon "determined policy and implementation in the (forestry) arena."
Kuhn, who will lead Monday's delegation, emphasised at the time that the government must follow through on promises to halt illegal logging and clean up its accounts with concrete action.

The IMF decision, coupled with growing concern from donors over heavy as well as illegal logging, has prompted the government to take some steps since then, including closing its borders to log exports.
In a meeting with donors last month, Agriculture Minister Tao Seng Huor said the government was enforcing the ban and seeking bids for an outside firm to help control the situation.

But the original firm chosen to control logging, Societe Generale de Surveillance of Switzerland, withdrew last month, citing concerns that it would be expected to act as an enforcement agency or paramilitary force.
To win back the confidence of the IMF, the government must overcome that setback as well as prove that it is making recommended reforms in all sectors, said analysts.
They cited accounting procedures, reform of the country's bloated armed forces and civil sector and improved tax collection as particularly important issues.
The country's reputation in the international donor community, and future aid from bilateral agencies that take their lead from the IMF, were among the issues at stake, the analysts said.
The stability of foreign reserves, which dropped to critical levels last year and threatened the stability of the Cambodian riel was also important, they added.
"It is no small amount of money for Cambodia," said one diplomat. "And the IMF is strict, not compassionate."
